Banger paper from Meta Superintelligence Labs on on-device agent models. (bookmark it) If you build agents that need to run locally, this one is worth your time. Muse Glimmer is an open 30B model, distilled from Meta's frontier model Muse Spark and designed to fit in 32 GB of VRAM. With 4-bit quantization and a speculative decoding head, it runs on a single RTX 5090. On MCPAtlas, it scores 75.5, against 54.2 for Gemma4-31B and 62.5 for Qwen3.6-27B. On SWE-Bench Pro, it scores 51.2, against 36.9 and 50.2. Qwen3.6-27B still leads on OSWorld-Verified and TerminalBench 2.1, so the gains are concentrated in tool use and long-horizon tasks. The model takes text and images, covers more than a hundred languages, and is released under Apache 2.0. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24628 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/muse-glimmer-30b-an-on-device-agentic-model-2610.24628

Is harness engineering dead? Absolutely NOT! Like the "prompt engineering is dead" and "RAG is dead" claims, this is just another misinformed claim used for clicks and ragebaiting. Mostly, it stems from a few recently published papers with poor experimental setups that focus only on SWE on already benchmaxxed SWE benchmarks. If we are talking about SWE, of course a lot of the harness stuff is getting absorbed by the model. And that's great. Thanks to better approaches for co-evolving harnesses and models. But in reality, you still need a stable, minimal harness to get high-quality results reliably and affordably. The big issue I see is that we assume SWE won't evolve. It already has, and as a result, teams are finding they need specialized harnesses to improve code review, cybersecurity, and work in more complex environments (multi-agent systems, sandboxes, etc.). The harness isn't just about prompts; it's the scaffolding that makes AI models work in the real world, covering security, safety guardrails, authorization, coordination, memory, scalable and new infra, efficiency, costs, and more. If you have been in computer science for long, none of these stay fixed. So how can anyone claim the scaffold/harness isn't needed? And worse, how can anyone claim these AI models will know all that, much of it proprietary and custom to every problem and domain? It gets more complex when you apply agents beyond SWE; domain-specific harnesses are popping up everywhere. These require entirely new ways to optimize context, memory, guardrails, security, and more. To make my point even clearer, look at the new wave of proactive and personal agents (Muse, Grok Bot, dots, Instinct, etc.). They involve clever, complex harness engineering. I think we will see vertical personal agents too, so the harness will get even more specialized. I can go on and on. I'd love to hear what other serious builders here are seeing.

Brilliant paper on scaling laws for agentic RL data. It's a great paper worth reading if you are synthesizing data for agentic RL. (bookmark it) They fit scaling laws for agentic RL data along three axes: tasks, environments, and trajectories. Across model sizes, families, domains, and both PPO and GRPO, the exponents order the same way, with environments above tasks and tasks above trajectories. The environment advantage seems to come mainly from world diversity, meaning genuinely different settings. Varying the structure of the same world helps about as much as adding tasks. The laws also give each synthesis method a discount factor and a synthetic-to-real ratio at which training starts to collapse. Those ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. In addition, allocating the budget with their recipe gives up to 1.7x compute efficiency over the common practice of generating more trajectories. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23946 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/how-data-scales-in-agentic-reinforcement-learning-laws-and-synthesis-strategies-2610.23946

Here's the full prompt to copy: 1. Here are customer reviews for [product]. Use only their words. Don't invent anything. 2. List the phrases they repeat about the problem they had before buying. 3. List the exact words they use to describe the result. Quote them word for word. 4. List every worry they mention, and what changed their mind. 5. Write 5 headlines and 5 ad hooks built from their exact phrases. 6. For each line, show the review it came from. Flag any claim we'd need to prove. Example: Review: "I finally sleep through the night without waking up sweaty" Headline: Finally sleep through the night. [paste reviews here] Tip: gather 50 to 100 reviews from every star rating. 5-star reviews give you the result words. 3-star reviews show the doubts and what changed their mind. 1 to 2-star reviews show the objections your ads need to answer.

Your customers already wrote your best ads. The AI prompt that finds them is in the reply. A few tips before you run it: - Support emails and post-purchase survey answers work too. Paste them in with the reviews. - Take out names and email addresses before you paste anything in. - Spot-check every quote against the original review before you use it. - Use what you find everywhere: ads, product pages, landing pages, and your homepage.
